Assign Values Passed at the Command Line or Interactively

Source: R/cmd_assign.R
cmd_assign.Rd

Assign names to values in the global environment. The values are typically supplied through the command line, but can be supplied interactively.

cmd_assign_quiet() is identical to cmd_assign() except that it does not print progress messages to the console.

Usage

cmd_assign(...)

cmd_assign_quiet(...)

Arguments

...

Name-value pairs.

Value

cmd_assign() is called for its side effect, which is to create objects in the global environment. However, cmd_assign() also invisibly returns a named list of objects.

Details

cmd_assign() is a user-friendly alternative to commandArgs(), designed specifically for data analysis workflows.

cmd_assign() can be used to record and enforce assumptions about inputs and outputs. This provides scripts with better-defined interfaces, making them clearer and safer.

Types of session

cmd_assign() behaves differently depending on whether it is called interactively, or from within an R script being run from the command line.

For instance, if the code

cmd_assign(use_log = TRUE)

is run interactively, it creates an object called use_log with value TRUE.

But if the same code is run from within a script that has been invoked using the command

Rscript tidy_data.R --use_log=FALSE

it creates an object called use_log with value FALSE.

cmd_assign() is typically called interactively when a workflow is being developed, and through the command line when the workflow is in production.

Matching names and values

When used in a script called from the command line, cmd_assign() first matches named command line arguments, and then matches unnamed command line arguments, in the order in which they are supplied.

If, for instance, the script person.R contains the lines

cmd_assign(
  .data = "raw_data.csv",
   max_age = 85,
   .out = "person.rds"
)

and if person.R is run from the command line using

Rscript person.R \
  raw_data.csv \
  person.rds \
  --max_age=100

then cmd_assign() assigns cmd_assign() names to command line arguments in the following order:

ordercmd_assign() namecommand line argument
1max_age--max_age=100
2.dataraw_data.csv
3.outperson.rds

The values specified in the call to cmd_assign() are not defaults

The values specified in the call to cmd_assign() are not defaults in the sense of values to fall back on when no value is supplied. For instance, if we take a script containing the call

cmd_assign(
  n_draw = 10,
  .out = "simulation.rds"
)

and run it from the command line without passing a value for n_draw, then cmd_assign() will throw an error. It will not set n_draw to 10.

Defaults can hide bugs and make code less predictable.

Coercing values passed at the command line

Values passed at the command line start out as text strings. cmd_assign() coerces these strings to have the same class as the corresponding values in the call to cmd_assign(). For instance, if script fit.R contains the lines

cmd_assign(
  .data = "data/individuals.rds",
  impute = TRUE,
  date = as.Date("2025-01-01"),
  .out = "output/fitted.rds"
)

and if fit.R is run from the command line using

Rscript src/fit.R \
  data/individuals.rds \
  output/fitted.rds \
  --impute=TRUE \
  --date=2025-01-01

then cmd_assign() will create the following length-1 vectors

nameclassvalue
.data"character""data/individuals.rds"
impute"logical"TRUE
date"Date""2025-01-01"
.out"character""output/fitted.rds"

The dot-name convention

When naming arguments to cmd_assign(), it is typically good practice to use names starting with dots for file paths, and names without dots for ordinary objects, as in

cmd_assign(
  .households = "data/households.csv",
  n_record = 500,
  sex = "Female",
  .out = "out/subsample_female.rds"
)

Function cmd_assign() does not in fact distinguish between names with dots and names without dots. But the dot-name convention is still useful because of the way it calls attention to the distinction between file paths and ordinary objects. For instance, a dot-name is a reminder that the object being named is a reference to an input or output, rather than the input or output itself.

In contrast, functions extract_make(), extract_shell(), makefile(), and shell_script() do treat names with dots differently from names without dots. See the help for extract_make(), extract_shell(), makefile(), and shell_script() for details.

Examples

if (interactive()) {
  cmd_assign(.data = "mydata.csv",
             n_iter = 2000,
             .out = "results.rds")
}
